title: Culture: An Introduction
summary: The English word 'culture' comes from the Latin 'cult' or 'cultus', meaning tilling, cultivating, refining and worship – practically the same as the Sanskrit 'Sanskriti', derived from the root 'Kri' (to do). From this root come prakriti (basic matter or condition), Sanskriti (refined matter) and vikriti (modified or decayed matter). Culture is a way of life: the food we eat, the clothes we wear, the language we speak and the God we worship; it is the embodiment of the way in which we think and do things, and the things we inherit as members of society – art, music, literature, architecture, sculpture, philosophy, religion and science. It is a human-made environment of material and non-material products of group life, transmitted from one generation to the next. It has two components: material culture (dress, food, household goods) and non-material culture (ideas, ideals, thoughts, beliefs). Culture varies from place to place.

Civilization means better ways of living, making nature serve our needs and organising societies politically for improved conditions of food, dress and communication; culture refers to the inner being, a refinement of head and heart – arts, sciences, music, dance and other higher pursuits. A poor person in cheap clothes may be the most cultured; a wealthy person may be civilized but not cultured. People live at physical, mental and spiritual levels; only when the deeper levels of intellect and consciousness find expression is one 'cultured'. 'Culture is what we are; civilization is what we possess or use.' Both change, and civilization is an advanced state of culture.

Cultural development is a historical process: ancestors learnt from predecessors, added their own experience and gave up what was not useful. The culture we inherit from our predecessors is our cultural heritage, existing at levels – humanity as a whole (world heritage) and the nation (national cultural heritage). Cultural heritage includes all aspects or values of culture transmitted from generation to generation, cherished, protected and maintained with unbroken continuity. Examples: Taj Mahal, Red Fort, Qutub Minar, Mysore Palace, Dilwara Jain temple, Golden Temple, Sanchi Stupa, Goa churches, India Gate; intellectual achievements such as the contributions of Baudhayan, Aryabhata and Bhaskaracharya (mathematics and astronomy), Kanad and Varahamihira (physics), Nagarjuna (chemistry), Susruta and Charak (medicine) and Patanjali (yoga); and the Vedas, Upanishads and Gita. Culture is liable to change, but our heritage does not.

Culture is learned and acquired (not inherited; learnt from family and society); shared by a group; cumulative (knowledge is passed on and added to); changing (some traits are lost when new ones are added); dynamic (never in a permanent state); gives a range of permissible behaviour patterns; diverse (interdependent parts forming a whole); and ideational (lays down an ideal pattern of behaviour expected for social acceptance).

Culture makes us human; it gives meaning to life through traditions, beliefs and a way of life from the most spiritual to the most material. Religious belief and its symbolic expression are fundamental, and interfaith dialogue is intercultural dialogue; in a global world we must know our own culture and others'. The three eternal and universal values of Truth, Beauty and Goodness are linked with culture: it brings us closer to truth through philosophy and religion, brings beauty through the arts and makes us ethical through love, tolerance and peace. Self-restraint in conduct and consideration for others' feelings and rights are the highest marks of culture.

vsa: Describe the meaning of the word 'Kri' of Sanskrit.
'Kri' means 'to do'. From this root come prakriti (basic matter or condition), Sanskriti (refined matter or condition, culture) and vikriti (modified, broken or decayed matter or condition).

The culture we inherit from our predecessors is cultural heritage: all aspects and values of culture transmitted from generation to generation, cherished, protected and maintained with unbroken continuity, such as monuments, knowledge and scriptures.
What is meant by civilization? Explain.

Civilization means better ways of living, bending nature to fulfil needs and organising societies into politically well-defined groups for improved food, dress and communication, as distinct from the inner refinement that is culture.
Give two differences between culture and civilization.

Culture is the inner refinement of head and heart (arts, sciences, values), civilization is outer better ways of living and use of nature; culture is what we are, civilization is what we possess or use.
Name two examples of cultural heritage of India.
Taj Mahal, Red Fort, Sanchi Stupa, Golden Temple; the Vedas, Upanishads and Gita (any two).
Mention two general characteristics of culture.
Culture is learned and acquired; it is shared, cumulative, dynamic, diverse and gives permissible behaviour patterns (any two).
sa: Describe three things which show one's culture.
Our language and way of speaking, our dress and food habits, and our greeting, customs and religious practices show our culture; so do the way we treat others, our art and our beliefs.

or: Describe three ways of our behaviour which pronounce our culture.
Self restraint in conduct; consideration for the feelings of others; respect for the rights of others, tolerance, love and peace.

sa: 'Culture refers to a human-made environment.' Explain the statement.

Culture includes all material (tools, dress, buildings) and non-material (ideas, beliefs, values) products of group life that human beings create and transmit from one generation to the next; it is not natural but made and learnt.

or: No culture remains in a permanent state; new ideas and techniques are constantly added, modifying or replacing old ways, which stems from its cumulative quality.

sa: Popular culture is the culture of the masses – music, films, dress, festivals and entertainment shared and enjoyed by large numbers of people in daily life.

sa: Why is it important to know our own culture as well as others'?
In a global world different cultures and beliefs must co-exist; we cannot dialogue with others unless we know our own culture; knowing other cultures builds tolerance and respect.
Explain the link between culture and heritage.

Culture develops through history as ancestors add and drop traits; what we inherit from them is our cultural heritage, which includes monuments, artefacts, knowledge, philosophy and scriptures; culture may change but the heritage remains.
la: Culture comes from Latin 'cult' meaning tilling or refining and equals the Sanskrit 'Sanskriti' from the root 'Kri'. It is a way of life: food, dress, language and religion are aspects of culture. It is the embodiment of the way we think and do things and the things we inherit as members of society – art, music, literature, architecture, sculpture, philosophy, religion and science. It is a human-made environment of material (dress, food, household goods) and non-material (ideas, beliefs) products, transmitted from generation to generation by symbols. It varies from place to place and has a historical development.
'Culture relates us with eternal and universal values.' Examine the statement.

Culture is closely linked with life; it is what makes us human. Three eternal and universal values – Truth, Beauty and Goodness – are linked with it. Culture brings us closer to truth through philosophy and religion; it brings beauty into our lives through the arts and makes us aesthetic beings; and it makes us ethical by bringing us closer to others and teaching love, tolerance and peace. It gives ideas, ideals and values for a decent life; self restraint and consideration for others' rights are its highest marks.
What are the universal characteristics of culture? Illustrate with examples.

Culture is learned and acquired (we learn language and manners from family); shared by a group; cumulative (knowledge is added over generations); changing and dynamic (new ideas and techniques replace old, e.g. dress); gives a range of permissible behaviour (how to greet elders); diverse with interdependent parts; and ideational, laying down ideal behaviour for social acceptance.
Explain the aspects of a civilization and how it differs from culture.

Civilization means better ways of living socially and politically and better use of nature – organised societies, food, dress and communication. Some groups consider themselves civilized and look down on others, which has led to wars. Culture is the inner refinement of head and heart – arts, sciences, music, dance and higher pursuits – and a poor person may be very cultured while a wealthy person may be civilized but not cultured. Culture is what we are, civilization what we possess.
